Kotlin Multiplatform, from the compiler up · Puzzle 11 · 12 of 16

Whose thread is it?

Your shared code uses coroutines and Dispatchers.Main. On Android, that's the main Looper. On iOS there's no Looper. Here's where your coroutines run, and the one thing Swift can't do to them.

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 10: The main thread on iOS

    iOS's main thread runs a run loop, the role of Android's Looper: it waits for work, handles it, and waits again. Work for it waits in the main queue, the role of the MessageQueue, and DispatchQueue.main.async plays handler.post. As on Android, UIKit may be touched only from the main thread, and slow work there freezes the screen.

The problem

In puzzle 6, a suspend function crossed into Swift as a function with a completion handler. Inside, your shared code launches coroutines on Dispatchers.Main and Dispatchers.IO, as it would on Android. On Android, Main means the main thread's Looper. An iPhone has no Looper. Which thread runs your coroutines on iOS, and what happens when the Swift side gives up? (A Swift Task is Swift's version of a launched coroutine, and await is where it waits.)

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

On iOS, Dispatchers.Main is backed by the main queue from puzzle 10, the line of tasks the main thread's run loop works through. So a coroutine that resumes on Dispatchers.Main runs on the main thread, exactly where screen work belongs, just as on Android. Dispatchers.Default and Dispatchers.IO run on Kotlin's own pools of worker threads.

The surprise is cancellation. On Android, cancelling a scope, the CoroutineScope that owns a group of coroutines, stops all of them. From Swift, a Kotlin suspend function arrives as a function with a completion handler, and that bridge has no way to pass a cancellation through. So when the Swift task that's waiting is cancelled, say the user leaves the screen, the Kotlin coroutine keeps going: the network call runs to the end, and the Swift side still waits for it, for a screen that's already gone.

Two ways out. Libraries such as SKIE, a Kotlin-to-Swift bridge from Touchlab, generate real Swift async functions that do pass cancellation through. Or your shared code owns the scope itself: a shared class creates its CoroutineScope, and exposes a close() that the Swift side calls when the screen goes away, which cancels everything in it.

The analogy

A restaurant kitchen. On iOS the head chef still works at the main counter (the main queue), and the prep cooks are still in the back. But when a diner on the Swift side walks out, nobody tells the kitchen: the order is cooked anyway, unless the kitchen itself is told to close the ticket.

Check yourself

Your shared code resumes a coroutine on Dispatchers.Main on iOS. Which thread runs it?

Right. Main is still the main thread on iOS.

Not quite. The dispatcher decides, not the caller: Main means the main queue.

Not quite. On iOS, Main is backed by the main queue, so it still runs on the main thread.

A Swift task awaits your suspend function, then is cancelled. You use no bridge library. What happens to the Kotlin coroutine?

Not quite. The plain bridge is a completion handler, which has no way to carry the cancellation across.

Right. Without a bridge, cancellation doesn't cross.

Not quite. Nothing pauses it; it runs to the end, and nothing stops it.

What's the difference between Dispatchers.Main on Android and on iOS?

Right. Different machinery, same thread.

Not quite. UIKit has a main thread too; Main runs there on both platforms.

Sources

  • kotlinx.coroutines API: Dispatchers.Main ("On Native Darwin-based targets, it is a dispatcher backed by Darwin's main queue.")
  • SKIE: Suspend functions ("suspend functions have to be exposed as Obj-C callback functions, which can be called from Swift using the async/await syntax. However, this is just Swift's syntax sugar. Swift still handles these functions as callback functions that do not support cancellation.")

What you now know

On iOS, Dispatchers.Main is backed by the main queue, so a coroutine resumed there runs on the main thread, like on Android. Default and IO run on Kotlin's own worker threads. If Swift calls a suspend function without a bridge library, cancelling the Swift task doesn't cancel the Kotlin coroutine, so the shared code must own the scope.
